title: Close the billing endpoints that list more than one permission

blocks.text: The billing API marks each endpoint with the permissions that let a caller in:

Holding any one of them is enough. A method that lists none uses its class's permissions, and an endpoint with none on the method or its class is public. The penetration test found that a caller with no billing permissions at all can call some protected endpoints, while others refuse them as they should.

`PermissionGuard.mayCall(...)` already applies those rules to whatever `required(...)` returns. Finish `required(Method endpoint)` in `src/main/java/practice/PermissionGuard.java`: it returns the permissions that let a caller into the endpoint, for an endpoint or a class that lists one permission or several. About five lines in total.

cases.says: a caller who holds the one permission an endpoint lists may call it
a caller who holds any one of several listed permissions may call the endpoint
an endpoint with no permissions on the method or its class is open to every caller
a permission written once on a class applies to its methods that list none
a method that lists two permissions refuses a caller who holds neither
a method that lists one permission refuses a caller who doesn't hold it
two permissions written on a class both apply to its methods, and a caller with neither is refused

origin.section: A Repeated Annotation Is Stored Inside Its Container

concepts: An annotation written more than once is stored inside its container, so getAnnotation finds either the single annotation or the container, and getAnnotationsByType finds every one.
